question: Should I take a rest day tomorrow?

answer.summary: Rova doesn't give advice on whether to rest or train, and can't tell that from wearable data. What the data does show is that your recent training sits within your usual range, and the one heavy stretch this month was Aug 16 – Aug 20.

observed.text: Training load averaged 54.0 over the last 7 days, within your usual range of 33.5 to 69.9. Training duration averaged 58.3 min, within your usual range of 35.5 min to 79.7 min.
Training load was above your usual range on five days in a row (72, 84, 91, 88 and 76), peaking at 91 on Aug 18. Training duration was also above range, with a high of 110 min on Aug 18.

During that same stretch, sleep duration, sleep score and HRV were below your usual range, while resting heart rate, temperature deviation and sleeping respiration were above it. These measures moved together.
Training was lighter on Aug 22 (load 20, 20 min) and Aug 23 (load 28, 26 min), both below your usual range. The last 7 days of sleep, HRV and resting heart rate were all within your usual ranges.

interpretation: The recent week looks closer to your normal pattern than the Aug 16 – Aug 20 stretch, which may mean your body measures have settled since then.
insufficientData: The file ends on Aug 30, so there is no data for the days after that or for today. Rova also can't see how you feel, and these measures can't show whether you need rest.
answer.boundary: Rova describes what your data shows; it doesn't give training, medical or treatment advice. The decision is yours, and a coach or healthcare professional can help with it.
answer.basis: Training load, training duration, and the other six measures for context, Aug 1 – Aug 30

question: Did hard training cause my bad sleep?

answer.summary: The data can't show that hard training caused your poorer sleep; it only shows they changed on the same days. Aug 16 – Aug 20 was your shortest and lowest-scoring sleep, and it coincided with your highest training load.

observed.text: Sleep duration was below your usual range (6.65 h to 7.78 h) every night, from 6.4 h on Aug 16 to a low of 5.8 h on Aug 19.
Sleep score was below your usual range (76.5 to 91.2) every night, with a low of 67 on Aug 19.
Training load was above your usual range (33.5 to 69.9), peaking at 91 on Aug 18, and training duration peaked at 110 min that day.

HRV was below, and resting heart rate, temperature deviation and sleeping respiration were above, their usual ranges on most of these days. Sleep duration was 7.4 h on Aug 21 and sleep score 84, back within your usual range.

knowledge.title: Moving together is not the same as causing
knowledge.text: When measures change on the same days, the data shows they coincided. It can't show that one caused the other, since things not in the data may explain both.

knowledge.title: Sleep score is your tracker's own measure
knowledge.text: Sleep score is your tracker's own calculation with no universal scale, so it is most useful compared with your own nights.

interpretation: The heavy training days and the short, lower-scoring nights may be linked, but they might also share another influence that isn't in this data.
Because several measures moved together during these five days, it could be one stretch of your body and routine being under strain, though the data can't say why.
insufficientData: The data can't show why your sleep dropped, or which came first. It doesn't record things like stress, schedule, or illness, and Rova can't tell from wearable data whether anything like that was involved.
answer.basis: Sleep duration, sleep score, training load, training duration, HRV, resting heart rate, temperature deviation and sleeping respiration, Aug 1 – Aug 30
